name: testing-gates
description: "The regression gates work lands through, by event: a batch's scoped gates, a wave's, a module's end or switch from C and a ship point's; campaign mode and packaging, sanitizers, BSan and Miri, rebases under the landing lock, and a port batch's export checks. Read before running a batch's gates, landing, integrating a module or shipping."
---

# Testing gates

The gates every landing passes, over the tests [`testing`](../SKILL.md) classifies and the
builds [`testing-builds`](../builds/SKILL.md) describes.

## 1. Regressions

Every batch checks, formats and lints the workspace on the tree it lands, with warnings
denied, as [`toolchain`](../../../rust/toolchain/SKILL.md) describes, and tests what its
change can affect: its module and the modules that depend on it, as `modules.json` records
them, each by its tests' module paths.

Every build of those gates runs in the raw bindings' campaign mode, as
[`bindgen`](../../../rust/bindgen/SKILL.md)'s Build modes section describes, so that each fails when the
committed bindings do not match their input. A batch that changed the raw bindings, or a
landing that changes `c/`, also packages the safe crate, built alone in bundled mode from
the C it packages, with no build variant selected. Until the out-of-tree wrappers are
published, each crate the package depends on is patched to its local source, so that the
package builds alone.

The tests run against the matching variant, or a private replacement, and each event runs
them to its own depth:

- a batch: the tests above, plain and under ASan/UBSan, and its own tests under each other
  sanitizer its items call for, such as TSan where it asserts `Send` or `Sync` or adds a
  threaded callback, or MSan where C leaves memory it hands over partly unwritten;
- a wave's end: the workspace's tests, and the Miri gate below;
- a module's end, its switch in a port: every test under every available sanitizer,
  and BSan as below; and
- a ship point: every gate over the whole workspace under every available sanitizer, with
  the coverage measurement.
<!-- TODO: a wave's end and a module's end are run by the wave's last review batch and the
module pass, so a campaign without review runs neither: they need an owner there. -->

BSan, when available, is run for every batch and at module end:

- For a batch, it runs only on the individual tests or reproducers the batch expects to
  trigger it, each by exact name and alone; never on a whole test binary, a suite or the
  workspace.
- At module end, it runs as a gate over everything the module landed: the
  whole workspace, one invocation per test binary, as many side by side as
  [`concurrency`](../../../operations/concurrency/SKILL.md) describes, each under a `timeout`.

A batch runs the tests it wrote under Miri. Miri is also run after every wave, as a gate
over the whole workspace: one Miri run on the pinned nightly per test binary, the library's
and each integration suite's, as many side by side as
[`concurrency`](../../../operations/concurrency/SKILL.md) describes, each skipping the
compile-fail tests. The gate passes only
with no Miri error: a test that stops at the foreign boundary without the attribute gets
it, and any other Miri error is a UB candidate of the item it touches.

`end-gates`, beside this skill and documented by its `--help`, runs a wave's and a
module's end gates so, over a snapshot of the tree, so that work goes on in the tree while
they run: the workspace under each variant, Miri and BSan per test binary, and the BSan
tests known never to finish skipped by name, each skip checked against its binary's test
list before anything runs.

Each gate run starts in the background and is waited on to exit; its output is neither
polled nor read while it runs. BSan reports false positives at the foreign boundary, so
only a true positive, a report that reproduces through the Rust side as a single test or
standalone reproducer, becomes a UB finding.

Every translation and review batch measures the consumer-facing API of its items against
the tip it rebased onto, each change classified as the dashboard's API stability columns
name them. An item's API is fixed by its first landing: a later landing
that changes or removes it, a port, a later stage, a rebind or a review fix alike, breaks
its consumers, and is kept only with its reason recorded in the batch's notes, such as a
soundness fix; the measure does not fail the gate. A module's integration measures every
item of the module against the module's base, and a ship point the whole crate against the
previous ship point.

When C changed, the configured C build and baseline run. A wrap-only batch with no C
change does not need the full C baseline.

A batch validates its own change on its own base first. Its rebase onto the integration
branch, under the landing lock that [`versioning`](../../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Landing section
describes, then combines that change with the work landed since: the gates run again are
those that could catch a regression the combination introduces, judged from what the
batch's change and the rebased-in changes touch and how they could interact. A gate that
neither side's changes could affect keeps the result it had, and a rebase that conflicts
makes the resolved tree new work of the batch's own.

A `port` batch changes no C: its gates are those above, run against the variants with its
module's export feature off, so that the ported Rust is tested beside the C it replaces.
It also checks and lints the safe crate with that feature on, which compiles the module's
gateway without linking it, and each export is checked at compile time against the raw
binding of the C declaration it replaces, so that a signature that drifts from C's fails
to build.

A module's switch removes its translation unit, and the C tests tied to it that reach
its internals, from `c/`, rebuilds the variants from the C that remains and deletes the
module's export feature, as
[`porting-workflow`](../../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section
describes. Its gates are a module's end's, in campaign mode over the rebuilt variants, and
the target's remaining C tests, which link the remaining C and the safe crate's Rust static
library, so that the C reaches the ported module through its exports: the module's tied C
tests that use only its public API among them, as the porting workflow's Tests follow
their modules section describes. Before a tied C test leaves, the cases none of the
module's `unit_pub` tests carries over are listed, as [`testing`](../SKILL.md)'s C tests
carried over section describes.

name: accounting
description: "The dashboard, its cells, the runs' records and transcripts, and how cost and time are derived. Read before filling dashboard cells or collecting a run's records."
---

# Accounting

What a campaign records about its own work: the dashboard, the runs' records and
transcripts its figures come from, and how cost and time are derived from them.

## 1. The dashboard

The dashboard, `crustify/artifacts/dashboard.md` unless the settings name another, is the
campaign's record of what each planner run, batch, wave and module did and cost. It is
filled from `templates/translate/dashboard.template.md`, an audit's from
`templates/audit/dashboard.template.md`, and keeps the template's format exactly.
When an adopted Crustify change adds a table or a column to the template, it is
added to the dashboard on the working branch before the next batch launches: a batch
fills the rows of the tables in place, and never adds one.

It is tracked in the campaign's tree, so every agent's worktree holds a copy, and it is
filled as the work lands rather than at the end. Each figure is measured once, where it is
produced: no suite or scan is rerun only to record one.

## 2. Cells

The dashboard's cells fall into three kinds, by when their figures can be known.

### 2.1 Landing cells

The cells measured on the tree a landing commits:

- for a batch, under the route its items' `kind` selects, as
  [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Routes section gives it: its rows
  in that route's `Batches`, tests, `Batches: safety audit` and `Batches: API stability` tables, and for a review batch in
  `Batches — review: PoC + reports`, each placed in module, wave and batch order under
  its `pass`, and for a module pass, which spans both routes, in `Module passes`; those
  tables' `Σ` rows; and the `Coverage stats` table and the Overview's LoC
  line;
- for a planner run, its row in `Planning`, but for its usage cells.

They are filled in the landing's last commit, and measured against the integration branch
tip it was rebased onto: coverage as [`testing-builds`](../../verification/testing/builds/SKILL.md)'s Coverage section measures
it, the safety audit columns as the changes in the dashboard's Safety audit metrics, and
the API stability columns as the changes to the API of the landing's items are classified. A
rebase that conflicts in the dashboard keeps every row both sides added, and the landing's
cells, `Σ` rows included, are measured again where the gates its rebase reruns cover them;
the others stand as measured on the batch's base.

An integration merge, and any merge of one branch into another, keeps every row both
sides added, and settles the rest so: an additive `Σ` cell is the sum over the merged
rows, ours plus theirs less the merge base's, and so are the Overview's `Rust LoC`
figures; a usage `Σ` cell, its per-unit cells included, sums only the rows that carry
usage, so that it is filled again with theirs; a coverage `Σ` cell, and the Overview's
`C LoC`, are the later landing's; and `Coverage stats` takes the merged suites' counts,
with the later landing's percentages until a gate measures the merged tree, which the
merge commit's message says. A table or section the template holds once is kept once,
with the rows of every copy, whether or not the merge conflicts there, and the merged
dashboard is checked for repeated headings before it is committed.

### 2.2 Usage cells

The cells known only once an agent has ended, from its usage: its cost, tokens and wall,
the per-unit costs derived from them, and their `Σ` cells. A batch's are filled on the
working branch once its row is there, once its module is integrated, as
[`versioning`](../versioning/SKILL.md) describes, or, for a port's later-stage batch, which
runs after its module's switch, once its wave is promoted. A planner run's are filled once the run is
promoted. A batch run more than once costs the sum of its runs.

### 2.3 Campaign cells

The cells that span agents: the `Module stats` table, the Overview's branch line and
test baseline, and the `Settings` lines. A module's row and the branch line are filled
when the module is integrated, and a port's module row again as each of its later-stage
waves is promoted, the baseline once it is recorded, and the `Settings` lines,
with a Notes entry, whenever a settings change is applied.

### 2.4 Side campaign cells

A side campaign keeps its own dashboard, in its own repository, and its figures are
measured there. The parent's `Side campaigns` table copies them, one row per wrapper, as
they stand at the commit the parent pins, and the `side campaigns` row of `Module stats`
sums the rows, so that the parent's `Σ campaign` covers what its side campaigns cost. A
wrapper's row is filled each time the parent's pin moves, and its `shipped at` cell when
the wrapper ships the commit the parent pins. A side campaign that serves several parents
appears in each, with the figures as of each one's pin.

An audit's dashboard follows the same kinds over its own tables.

## 3. Records

Every run's `task.json` records how its agent ran: its backend, billing, model proxy and
the arguments its CLI was given, and, once it starts, its `session_id`, which ties the run
to its session. The session's transcript, which its CLI keeps by session id, is the
agent's full log and the source of its accounting. An agent spawned as a subagent of
another session has no session of its own: its session id is `agent-<agent id>`, the
name its host gives its transcript, under the spawning session's `subagents/`.

A transcript is copied into crustify's home, as `transcripts/<session id>.jsonl`, as soon
as its agent ends, because the CLIs move and prune their own files. Its usage is derived
from the copy, as [`usage`](../usage/SKILL.md) describes, with the backend and model proxy its
`task.json` names.

An evolution review is a run like any other: its `task.json` sits in its artifact dir, and
its transcript is collected and priced the same way, its cost counted with the sessions that
orchestrate the campaign and recorded, with its tokens and wall time, in its proposal's
Review section, so that what each review bought can be weighed against its cost.

The sessions that orchestrate the campaign are collected the same way: at the start of each session, the
transcripts of the sessions before it. A resumed session keeps its id while its transcript
grows: its transcript is copied again after each run, replacing the earlier copy. The
records, transcripts and rates stay in crustify's home.

## 4. Cost and time

A run's cost and tokens are its usage's `total.cost_usd` and `total.tokens`, as
[`usage`](../usage/SKILL.md) derives them from its transcript. The computed cost is used, never a provider-reported
dollar total; under subscription billing it is the API-equivalent cost.

An agent's wall time is its usage's interval. A wave's runs from its first batch's
launch through its final review and regression gates, a review wave's in an audit through
its landing, and a module's from its first launch through its final gate.

name: porting-workflow
description: "The principles a port campaign follows and where it differs from binding: Rust consumers, tests tied to modules, one language per module, a module's switch from C to Rust and its builds. Read before porting a module or integrating one."
---

# Porting workflow

How a `port` campaign proceeds. It follows the [binding workflow](../binding-workflow/SKILL.md) throughout;
this document gives the principles a port follows and where it differs. How each item is
ported is [`porting`](../../rust/porting/SKILL.md).

## 1. Principles

### 1.1 Rust consumers

A port produces a Rust library for Rust-native applications. Its public API is the safe
Rust one; the installed C headers and the C ABI they describe are not kept for C
applications outside the target. The crate bundles the C that remains, as
[`bindgen`](../../rust/bindgen/SKILL.md) describes, so that a consumer has the whole
library and reaches what is not ported yet through its raw bindings.

A ported module's C-facing surface is only what the target's own remaining C still
consumes, its translation units, tests and executables alike: its `extern "C"` exports,
under their bare C names, through which that C calls the Rust that replaced the module. The
remaining C depends on the Rust, never the Rust on a C copy of a ported module, so that
each function has one implementation and each global one copy. The surface shrinks as that
C is ported.

A type, public or internal, therefore keeps its C layout, and its `wrap`, only while
unported C of the target accesses that layout. The target's tests do not count, as
[Tests follow their modules](#12-tests-follow-their-modules) describes, and neither does a
definition in an installed header: the C consumers it would serve are outside the target.

### 1.2 Tests follow their modules

Each module carries the C tests tied to it, those whose subject it is, as
[`decomposition`](../../planning/decomposition/SKILL.md)'s Bundling section describes.
They assert the C contract, which a safe Rust implementation may change. Those that reach
the module's internals run while it is C and leave with it at its switch. Those that
use only its public API stay, and check its exports, which keep that contract for the C
that calls them, until their `port/unexport` carries them over, as the
[conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md)' Exports section describes. The tests its
port batches write mirror their regression cases, as
[`testing`](../../verification/testing/SKILL.md)'s C tests carried over section describes. A
test's access to a module's internals is a use within that module, so it never keeps a type
wrapped.

A C test that only calls a module, to set up or tear down its fixtures, is not tied to it:
once the module has switched, the test reaches it through its exports, so that it checks
its own subject with the ported Rust under it, as part of the integration regression gate. A
test never keeps an export the remaining C no longer needs: the export's `port/unexport`
carries over the test cases that still reference it, as
[`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages section describes.

A test whose subject is several modules is tied to each of them, and leaves at the first
point at which it would leave as a test of one of them alone. Each ported module's own
tests cover it from then on.

A test case whose body the configured build compiles empty, under a configuration the
target is built without, such as `GIT_WIN32`, tests nothing of the target: it is out of
scope, as a configured-out translation unit is, tied to no module and holding nothing back.

### 1.3 One language per module

A module is in one language at a time. The campaign maintains C and Rust side by side, but
on disjoint modules, never the same code in both.

While the waves of a module's `wrap` and `port` items run, its C is the reference its
ports are tested against, and the target is built and linked from C alone.
Once the last of them has landed, the module switches to Rust, once, as [Builds](#3-builds)
describes: the Rust module replaces the TU in the target's link, its C is removed from the
build and from the tree, and its tests switch with it. The removal is made on the working branch; the shipping branch keeps the C until
the user approves shipping the module. From then on the module is Rust's: what it still
keeps for the remaining C, its types' C layouts and storage and its exports, its later
stages remove after the switch, as [Later stages](#4-later-stages) describes.

The headers bundled with the module stay while remaining C includes them, declaring the
module's exports, its `static inline` functions included, as
[`porting-symbols`](../../rust/porting/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Static inline functions section describes, and go with the last C
file that includes them.

The module's equivalence tests, which need the C, are retired with it, and the behaviour
they established is kept by its unit tests. The raw bindings of its
exported functions and globals then reach its exports, so that a consumer's raw calls keep
working, and an allowlist entry goes with the export it reaches. Those of its functions and
globals that have no export, which only its own C referenced, are removed with their
allowlist entries at the switch.

A ported module's items therefore reach the rest of its module natively from the start:
an edge within a module needs neither a `wrap` binding nor an export, only the edges that
leave it.

## 2. Batches

A port campaign's schedule mixes both kinds of batch, as [`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s
Waves and batches section describes: a selected symbol is `port` from the start, a
selected type is `wrap` while another module's unported C depends on its layout and `port`
once none does, and a dependency outside the selected migration set stays `wrap`. A type
whose layout only its own module and tests use is `port` from the start. Each batch runs
the agent its objective names, in the same waves.

## 3. Builds

A module's waves do not change the compiled target. Its `port` batches add Rust that is
built and tested on its own, against the target's C build, which still compiles the
module's C and links no Rust: there is no build switch, and no batch flips one. The
module's `ffi_export` gateway is written with its items but compiled only under its export
feature, as the [conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md)' Exports and Export features sections
describe, which stays off, so its bare-named exports never collide with the C the tests
link. Native Rust items carry mangled names and cannot collide with it.

The C stays until the switch: the target's other C still calls the module's symbols, which
only the exports could define, and the module's equivalence tests and its cut cycles still
run through it.

Once the last wave of the module's `wrap` and `port` items has landed, it switches
in one step, with concurrent modules as part of its branch's integration into the working
branch, as [`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Integration section
describes: its export feature is deleted, so that its gateway compiles from then on, its TU
and the C tests tied to it that reach its internals are removed from `c/`, and the
remaining C reaches the module through its exports. The C side of the
step is a commit on the fork's `main`, as
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Repositories section
describes, and the campaign's commit records the submodule at it: integrations run one at a
time, so the two repositories move together. The shared variants are rebuilt from the C
that remains once the integration lands.

From then on, the C that remains is linked in two ways, and no process holds a module both
as C and as Rust, nor its Rust twice:

- a Rust consumer, the campaign's own tests included, links the safe crate and the C that
  remains, which the crate bundles, statically or as shared libraries, as the raw bindings'
  Build modes describe; and
- the target's remaining C consumers, its C tests and executables, link the C that remains
  and the safe crate's Rust static library, built in campaign mode so that it carries no C
  of its own, through the target's actual build system.

The C tests that remain run over that second link as the integration regression gate, as
[`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section describes.
For that link, the first switch changes the fork's C build so that the remaining C's
tests and executables link the safe crate's Rust library, static or shared, in the build
system's own idiom, and each later switch takes its module's C out of that build.

## 4. Later stages

A module switches once. Its later-stage waves, `port/layout`, `port/memory` and
`port/unexport`, run after its switch, each once the switches its release point
waits for have landed, as [`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages
section times them: as the remaining C stops using its types' layouts and storage and
calling its exports, they nativize the types and remove the exports. They belong to no run
of the module and integrate nothing: each forks from the working branch and is promoted
back to it, as [`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Lifecycle section
describes, and changes no C, since the C that held it back has left the build.

## 5. Scope

The unit of a port is a module: its scope is whole modules, the foundational ones
included, which stay `wrap`, as
[`decomposition`](../../planning/decomposition/SKILL.md)'s Foundational modules section
describes. Porting a few named items without their module is not described.

name: testing
description: "How work is tested: test kinds and suites, test objects, how thoroughly a wrapper is tested, UB tests under sanitizers and Miri, equivalence and unit tests, and the C tests carried over; testing-builds and testing-gates give the builds, coverage and gates. Read before writing tests."
---

# Testing

Tests are classified by what decides them and by the side of a module they test, and each
is placed where the conventions' Testing section places tests of its kind:

- UB tests on the safe public interface show that it does not reach UB, mainly by not
  triggering sanitizer or Miri crashes, or by failing to compile for a given illegal path;
- UB tests on the unsafe public interface target UB there: each public `unsafe fn` or
  method a workset adds, called within its stated `# Safety` contract, edge cases
  included. Raw `sys::` round-trips are not UB tests on the unsafe interface; they are unit
  or equivalence tests;
- equivalence tests show that the Rust behaves as the C it translates, mainly by passing
  equivalence assertions: `equiv_pub` on the module's exported API, `equiv_priv` on its
  internals; and
- unit tests show that the Rust keeps its contract, by passing Rust assertions, without
  the C: `unit_pub` on the public interface, `unit_priv` on the internal routines.

<!-- TODO: fuzzing, of the safe public interface and differentially against the C, is
deferred. -->

Test objects are constructed through safe constructors. The UB tests on the safe public
interface use the safe API alone, their suite forbidding `unsafe_code` at its root: a type
that no safe constructor or producer yields yet gets those tests in the batch that wraps
its first one. Elsewhere, while a type has no safe constructor, one documented unsafe
fixture per type adopts the raw constructor's result, and is replaced once the safe
constructor exists.

A test exercises the safe API wherever it can, so that the later stages of a port, which
keep that API, keep it passing. A test of a C form an item keeps, such as an unsafe
adoption, a function pointer's unsafe constructor, a trampoline or an export, goes with
the stage that removes the form.

How thoroughly a wrapper is tested follows how long it lasts. One a port will replace, a
type wrapped ahead of its port or a dependency whose module will be ported, keeps its safe
API through the port: it gets the tests of its public interface, which outlive it, and
none of its internals. A permanent one, every wrapper of a wrap campaign, the foundational
modules' and one whose later stage is held back for good, gets every kind.

The builds the tests run against and how coverage is measured are
[`testing-builds`](builds/SKILL.md)'s, and the gates every landing passes
[`testing-gates`](gates/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. UB tests

UB tests show that a workset's public API is free of UB.

The unsafe public interface is tested with one suite per public unsafe function or method
a workset adds, its inputs built through the safe API wherever one exists. A workset that
adds no public unsafe API has no UB tests on the unsafe interface.

The sanitizers available are those the campaign built: the instrumented variants of
`crustify/artifacts/build.json`, where `asan-ubsan` provides ASan and UBSan, `msan` MSan, `tsan` TSan
and `bsan` BSan. A sanitizer without a variant is not available, so no test is written for
it and none runs under it. Miri needs no C build and is always available.

A target that ships its own sanitizers, because the standard ones cannot run against it,
is tested with those instead, each standing for the sanitizer it implements.

Each available sanitizer is a separate obligation of an item while it reaches C or unsafe
code; once it reaches neither, as a port's later stages bring about, Miri covers it alone:

  pointer/alignment UB, and integer/division/shift UB.

  uninitialized bytes crossing the FFI boundary, and struct tails or buffers a foreign
  initializer left partly unwritten. Its build instruments every component, the standard
  library through `-Zbuild-std` included: memory written by uninstrumented code reads as
  uninitialized, so a partial build reports falsely.
- BSan: conflicting foreign writes and retained foreign pointers across Rust reborrows.
  These tests are written like the others. BSan is the slowest instrument and reports
  false positives at the foreign boundary, so it runs only as
  [`testing-gates`](gates/SKILL.md)' Regressions section describes.

  implementation and threaded callback.
- Miri: Rust-side lifetime, bounds, initialization, validity, alignment, intrinsic, and
  `repr` assumptions. Miri cannot call the foreign library, read its globals or spawn a
  process, so every test that cannot run under it carries
  `#[cfg_attr(miri, ignore = "<reason>")]` on its test function, naming what stops it:
  `"calls C"`, `"reads a C global"`, and so on. A test is marked only after it was run
  alone under Miri and seen to stop there; never to silence a Miri report of undefined
  behaviour, a panic or a failed assertion, which are findings. The mark goes once what it
  names no longer stops the test, as a module's switch or a later stage brings about. Neither
  `#[cfg(not(miri))]` nor test-name filters stand in for the attribute: with it in place,

which ASan's runtime makes by default, nor Miri's leak check is a UB candidate.

UB tests exercise every owner and borrowed form, shared and mutable access path, lifecycle
strategy, generic instance, and callback variant a batch emits. They attempt to outlive the
owner, alias a reborrow, reenter a callback, and drop a parent first. Storage that C and
Rust both allocate or free, or whose allocator a port moves, is tested for a free through
the wrong allocator.

When the type system should reject a program, the test is a compile-fail doctest or a
`trybuild` case.

## 2. Equivalence tests

Equivalence tests run the C and the Rust that translates it on independently owned inputs
built from one description, and compare:

- return values and errors;
- out-parameters and buffers;
- callbacks;
- state transitions; and
- lifecycle effects.

They use multi-call sequences and compare after each step; single calls are only a
baseline.

The C side of a test meets the preconditions the C sets its callers, as the wrapper meets
them before its own calls: a library's global initialisation, which writes state its
routines read without synchronisation, runs before the test's first call that reads it,
since the harness runs other tests beside it on other threads.

They compare what the C specifies, through the mapping the safe API applies to it, such as
its status returns as errors and its null pointers as absent values, and not what it leaves
unspecified, such as an iteration order, a message's text, a pointer's value or an
allocation count. A confirmed C defect is not copied into Rust. The divergence is
documented, equivalence tests are retained for the unaffected behaviour, and the
corrected-behaviour regression is a unit test.

`equiv_pub` holds the module's exported API to the C strictly. `equiv_priv` compares an
internal routine with its C counterpart only where one exists, since an idiomatic port may
restructure the internals; a C function the raw bindings do not reach, one with internal
linkage, is compared through the functions that call it.

In a port, equivalence tests are the evidence of a module's migration. While its waves run,
the variants still build its C, which they reach through the raw bindings while the ported
Rust runs under its own names; at its switch they are retired with the C, and the
module evolves as Rust from then on, as
[`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Principles section
describes. Only its exports still keep the C contract, which the C tests that stay check.

## 3. Unit tests

A unit test is the right kind when Rust assertions supply the verdict: `unit_pub` on the
public interface, whose tests outlive the C, and `unit_priv` on internal facilities,
including:

- Rust-only `Iterator`, `Debug`, `Clone`, conversions, and builders;
- input rejected by Rust before FFI, including the error and no panic;
- deliberate correction of defective C behaviour;
- unsafe adoption through `from_raw`, `from_ptr`, or similar constructors;
- private or `pub(crate)` constructors and internal destructor/drop plumbing; and
- resource release exercised through any of those raw, unsafe, or internal paths.

## 4. C tests carried over

The `unit_pub` tests the port batches write for a module's items mirror the regression
cases of the C tests tied to it: their inputs, edge cases and call sequences, with the
assertions adapted to the safe Rust contract, so that what the C suites established
outlives them. Each names the C test case it carries over, so that before a C test
leaves, at the module's switch or with the exports it calls, the cases none carries
over are listed, and each is carried over or recorded as behaviour the safe API
deliberately changes. A `port/unexport` carries over every C test case that still references the
export it removes, whatever its subject, as a Rust test of that subject, reaching what is
still C through its wrappers, and removes the case from `c/`.

# Porting workflow

How a `port` campaign proceeds. It follows the [binding workflow](../binding-workflow/SKILL.md) throughout;
this document gives the principles a port follows and where it differs. How each item is
ported is [`porting`](../../rust/porting/SKILL.md).

## 1. Principles

### 1.1 Rust consumers

A port produces a Rust library for Rust-native applications. Its public API is the safe
Rust one; the installed C headers and the C ABI they describe are not kept for C
applications outside the target. The crate bundles the C that remains, as
[`bindgen`](../../rust/bindgen/SKILL.md) describes, so that a consumer has the whole
library and reaches what is not ported yet through its raw bindings.

A ported module's C-facing surface is only what the target's own remaining C still
consumes, its translation units, tests and executables alike: its `extern "C"` exports,
under their bare C names, through which that C calls the Rust that replaced the module. The
remaining C depends on the Rust, never the Rust on a C copy of a ported module, so that
each function has one implementation and each global one copy. The surface shrinks as that
C is ported.

A type, public or internal, therefore keeps its C layout, and its `wrap`, only while
unported C of the target accesses that layout. The target's tests do not count, as
[Tests follow their modules](#12-tests-follow-their-modules) describes, and neither does a
definition in an installed header: the C consumers it would serve are outside the target.

### 1.2 Tests follow their modules

Each module carries the C tests tied to it, those whose subject it is, as
[`decomposition`](../../planning/decomposition/SKILL.md)'s Bundling section describes.
They assert the C contract, which a safe Rust implementation may change. Those that reach
the module's internals run while it is C and leave with it at its switch. Those that
use only its public API stay, and check its exports, which keep that contract for the C
that calls them, until their `port/unexport` carries them over, as the
[conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md)' Exports section describes. The tests its
port batches write mirror their regression cases, as
[`testing`](../../verification/testing/SKILL.md)'s C tests carried over section describes. A
test's access to a module's internals is a use within that module, so it never keeps a type
wrapped.

A C test that only calls a module, to set up or tear down its fixtures, is not tied to it:
once the module has switched, the test reaches it through its exports, so that it checks
its own subject with the ported Rust under it, as part of the integration regression gate. A
test never keeps an export the remaining C no longer needs: the export's `port/unexport`
carries over the test cases that still reference it, as
[`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages section describes.

A test whose subject is several modules is tied to each of them, and leaves at the first
point at which it would leave as a test of one of them alone. Each ported module's own
tests cover it from then on.

A test case whose body the configured build compiles empty, under a configuration the
target is built without, such as `GIT_WIN32`, tests nothing of the target: it is out of
scope, as a configured-out translation unit is, tied to no module and holding nothing back.

### 1.3 One language per module

A module is in one language at a time. The campaign maintains C and Rust side by side, but
on disjoint modules, never the same code in both.

While the waves of a module's `wrap` and `port` items run, its C is the reference its
ports are tested against, and the target is built and linked from C alone.
Once the last of them has landed, the module switches to Rust, once, as [Builds](#3-builds)
describes: the Rust module replaces the TU in the target's link, its C is removed from the
build and from the tree, and its tests switch with it. The removal is made on the working branch; the shipping branch keeps the C until
the user approves shipping the module. From then on the module is Rust's: what it still
keeps for the remaining C, its types' C layouts and storage and its exports, its later
stages remove after the switch, as [Later stages](#4-later-stages) describes.

The headers bundled with the module stay while remaining C includes them, declaring the
module's exports, its `static inline` functions included, as
[`porting-symbols`](../../rust/porting/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Static inline functions section describes, and go with the last C
file that includes them.

The module's equivalence tests, which need the C, are retired with it, and the behaviour
they established is kept by its unit tests. The raw bindings of its
exported functions and globals then reach its exports, so that a consumer's raw calls keep
working, and an allowlist entry goes with the export it reaches. Those of its functions and
globals that have no export, which only its own C referenced, are removed with their
allowlist entries at the switch.

A ported module's items therefore reach the rest of its module natively from the start:
an edge within a module needs neither a `wrap` binding nor an export, only the edges that
leave it.

## 2. Batches

A port campaign's schedule mixes both kinds of batch, as [`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s
Waves and batches section describes: a selected symbol is `port` from the start, a
selected type is `wrap` while another module's unported C depends on its layout and `port`
once none does, and a dependency outside the selected migration set stays `wrap`. A type
whose layout only its own module and tests use is `port` from the start. Each batch runs
the agent its objective names, in the same waves.

## 3. Builds

A module's waves do not change the compiled target. Its `port` batches add Rust that is
built and tested on its own, against the target's C build, which still compiles the
module's C and links no Rust: there is no build switch, and no batch flips one. The
module's `ffi_export` gateway is written with its items but compiled only under its export
feature, as the [conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md)' Exports and Export features sections
describe, which stays off, so its bare-named exports never collide with the C the tests
link. Native Rust items carry mangled names and cannot collide with it.

The C stays until the switch: the target's other C still calls the module's symbols, which
only the exports could define, and the module's equivalence tests and its cut cycles still
run through it.

Once the last wave of the module's `wrap` and `port` items has landed, it switches
in one step, with concurrent modules as part of its branch's integration into the working
branch, as [`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Integration section
describes: its export feature is deleted, so that its gateway compiles from then on, its TU
and the C tests tied to it that reach its internals are removed from `c/`, and the
remaining C reaches the module through its exports. The C side of the
step is a commit on the fork's `main`, as
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Repositories section
describes, and the campaign's commit records the submodule at it: integrations run one at a
time, so the two repositories move together. The shared variants are rebuilt from the C
that remains once the integration lands.

From then on, the C that remains is linked in two ways, and no process holds a module both
as C and as Rust, nor its Rust twice:

- a Rust consumer, the campaign's own tests included, links the safe crate and the C that
  remains, which the crate bundles, statically or as shared libraries, as the raw bindings'
  Build modes describe; and
- the target's remaining C consumers, its C tests and executables, link the C that remains
  and the safe crate's Rust static library, built in campaign mode so that it carries no C
  of its own, through the target's actual build system.

The C tests that remain run over that second link as the integration regression gate, as
[`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section describes.
For that link, the first switch changes the fork's C build so that the remaining C's
tests and executables link the safe crate's Rust library, static or shared, in the build
system's own idiom, and each later switch takes its module's C out of that build.

## 4. Later stages

A module switches once. Its later-stage waves, `port/layout`, `port/memory` and
`port/unexport`, run after its switch, each once the switches its release point
waits for have landed, as [`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages
section times them: as the remaining C stops using its types' layouts and storage and
calling its exports, they nativize the types and remove the exports. They belong to no run
of the module and integrate nothing: each forks from the working branch and is promoted
back to it, as [`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Lifecycle section
describes, and changes no C, since the C that held it back has left the build.

## 5. Scope

The unit of a port is a module: its scope is whole modules, the foundational ones
included, which stay `wrap`, as
[`decomposition`](../../planning/decomposition/SKILL.md)'s Foundational modules section
describes. Porting a few named items without their module is not described.

out, all relative to the repository's root:

- `Cargo.toml` - the safe crate's manifest, which also declares the workspace.
- `src/lib.rs` - the safe crate's root, with one `cfg`-gated module per link unit.
- `src/<link-unit>/` - one sub-dir per link unit.
- `src/sys.rs` and `sys/<link-unit>/` - the raw bindings, one public module per link unit,
  laid out as [`bindgen`](../bindgen/SKILL.md) describes.

The safe crate is named after its repository, `<repo>-crustify`, as
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Repositories section names it:
a name crates.io leaves free, which tells it apart from the source's own Rust bindings,
such as `git2` for libgit2.

Within a link unit's sub-dir, the tree follows the module decomposition in `modules.json`
exactly, and preserves the C layout as far as the idiomatic organization of a Rust tree
allows:

- each module is one `.rs` file, at its translation unit's path below the C root with the
  `.rs` extension: its TU and the headers bundled with it have no files of their own,
  since Rust has no headers;
- a header module is one `<stem>_h.rs` file, at its header's path;
- the two modules of a split foundational TU share the TU's file;
- C directories become Rust modules: a directory's `.rs` file sits beside the directory,
  as `<dir>.rs` and `<dir>/`, and declares the modules within it, or is the module of a TU
  with the directory's name where there is one; `mod.rs` files are not used; and
- a file or directory name that is not a Rust identifier is sanitized, hyphens to
  underscores, and a Rust keyword takes a trailing underscore.

Where a C layout has no idiomatic Rust counterpart, the tree adapts it in the conventional
Rust way and keeps the C path recognizable. A batch names the `.rs` file each of its items
belongs in, as `src/<link-unit>/…/<file>.rs`. Entities sharing a
definition site co-home. A home may be shared across waves.

### 2.1 Unsafe regions

A module's unsafe code is confined to at most two inline child modules of its file, its
unsafe regions, so that the rest of the file, its native code, holds none:

- `mod ffi_import`: what the module reaches in C: its calls through the raw bindings, the C
  layouts it wraps with their handles and accessors, the owners and lifecycle policies over
  C's allocator, and the trampolines and contexts through which C calls a Rust closure
  back; and
- `mod ffi_export { use super::*; … }`: the gateway through which C reaches the module by
  symbol, as [Exports](#14-exports) describes, compiled only under its
  [export feature](#15-export-features).

Unsafe code is every `unsafe` block, `unsafe fn`, `unsafe impl`, `unsafe extern` block and
`#[unsafe(…)]` attribute, and every invocation of another crate's macro that expands to
one, such as one that mints a type over a C layout, which the compiler's `unsafe_code` lint does not
see. Outside the regions, only the raw bindings hold any. The regions take the lint back as
[`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s Unsafe code section describes.

A region exposes to its module only what [`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary
section lets it expose, and the module re-exports the public items a region defines, as
`pub use ffi_import::{Foo, FooBox, FooMut, FooRef};`, so that their paths do not depend on
which side defines them. A type's inherent `impl` blocks may be split between the native
code and a region: each method is visible as its own visibility says, counted from the
module that holds its block, so that a region's private helpers stay hidden from the
native code.

A region exists only while it holds something. A wrap's items are in `ffi_import`. A port
writes its item in the native code, and keeps in the regions only the C form the item
keeps, as [`porting`](../porting/SKILL.md) describes; a wrapped item it ports leaves
`ffi_import` with its re-export. The later stages empty the regions part by part: an
item's C layout and C owners leave `ffi_import` with its `port/layout` and `port/memory`,
its export leaves `ffi_export` with its `port/unexport`. A module without either region is
native, and its file carries `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`.

## 3. Anchors

## 4. Macros

A C macro is bound to a Rust form of its own:

- a type-generating macro, to one generic type, through [`binding-types`](../types/SKILL.md),
  its instances aliases of it;
- a constant macro, to a `const`, defined from its generated binding;
- a symbol alias, through the safe wrapper of the symbol it names, each of whose stand-ins
  stands in for the alias too and carries its anchor beside the symbol's own: where the
  symbol is a lifecycle primitive, the strategy methods that call it, as
  [Lifecycle strategies](#5-lifecycle-strategies) describes; and
- a macro that implements logic, to a function, `#[inline]`, or `const` where its body
  computes on its arguments alone, which reimplements the body and reaches C only for the
  symbols its expansion uses, through their safe wrappers, and for the fields it accesses,
  through their accessors. A `macro_rules!` takes its place only where a function cannot
  express it: control flow that leaves its caller, token pasting or stringification, an
  argument used as a place, or one evaluated lazily or more than once.

A macro whose expansion depends on the build's configuration, which the Rust does not see,
is the exception: it is reached through a shim, `crustify_<NAME>`, bound and wrapped.

## 5. Lifecycle strategies

A type's own lifecycle routines are bound with the type, as
[`binding-types`](../types/SKILL.md)'s Lifecycle section describes. The foundational
modules hold the rest: the allocators or constructors, releasers, disposers and cloners of
type-erased memory and of strings, each with the lifecycle role established while
planning, as [`decomposition`](../../../planning/decomposition/SKILL.md)'s Foundational
modules section describes. The analysis confirms each role from the item's body, and a role
the body contradicts is corrected, the correction recorded with the batch.

In a foundational module's batch, an item with a lifecycle role becomes a generic policy
or strategy that calls the primitive, through which the owners of strings and of
type-erased singletons and arrays allocate, clone and release what they hold, so that each
owner frees what it holds through the family that allocated it. The primitive itself is
not also exposed as an ordinary safe function. The module's other items follow their
route.

Singleton and array handles have separate policies, each in its primitive's home. A
family's allocator, releaser and cloner form one policy. A releaser that frees a container together with its
elements is no policy of the container: where its body only releases each element and then
the container, the owner holds its elements as their own owners, under the container's
allocator's policy, and releases as the releaser does without calling it; where it does
more, the owner is hand-written.

type-erased memory and of strings, each with the lifecycle role established while
planning, as [`decomposition`](../../../planning/decomposition/SKILL.md)'s Foundational
modules section describes. The analysis confirms each role from the item's body, and a role
the body contradicts is corrected, the correction recorded with the batch.

In a foundational module's batch, an item with a lifecycle role becomes a generic policy
or strategy that calls the primitive, through which the owners of strings and of
type-erased singletons and arrays allocate, clone and release what they hold, so that each
owner frees what it holds through the family that allocated it. The primitive itself is
not also exposed as an ordinary safe function. The module's other items follow their
route.

Singleton and array handles have separate policies, each in its primitive's home. A
family's allocator, releaser and cloner form one policy. A releaser that frees a container together with its
elements is no policy of the container: where its body only releases each element and then
the container, the owner holds its elements as their own owners, under the container's
allocator's policy, and releases as the releaser does without calling it; where it does
more, the owner is hand-written.

145:## 5. Lifecycle strategies
## 1. Functions

A function is bound as a `pub fn`; it is a `pub unsafe fn` only when no safe type-level
contract can express its caller obligation. Its FFI call, and the raw pointers it
reconstructs for it, sit in its module's `ffi_import` region, as the
[conventions](../../conventions/SKILL.md)' Unsafe regions section describes.

Its signature follows the analysis's findings, each argument and return taking the safe
form of what it names:

- **Out-parameters.** A pointer the function only writes through, to hand back a result,
  is part of the return, several of them a tuple, present only in the outcome in which the
  function writes it.
- **Buffers.** A pointer and the count that bounds it are one slice, the count taken from
  it; a buffer the function fills returns the part it filled.
- **Strings.** A NUL-terminated string the function borrows for the call is a borrowed C
  string, or the Rust string or path type of the encoding the analysis establishes,
  converted at the call, an interior NUL rejected before it. A returned string is a borrow
  tied to what keeps it alive, or an owner over its releaser where the caller frees it.
- **Nullability.** A nullable pointer is an `Option`.
- **Errors.** A function that can fail returns a `Result`, its failure read from the error
  convention the analysis establishes: a status return, a sentinel return, or error state
  the library keeps beside the call, read immediately after it, before another call into
  the library can replace it. A return that reports only success is not returned, and an
  outcome its C callers treat as ordinary, such as an exhausted iteration or an absent
  entry, is part of the success value. Each error convention has one error type, carrying
  what the convention reports, `errno`'s being `std::io::Error`.
- **Variadics.** A variadic function is bound through fixed-arity forms: one that formats
  its arguments takes the formatted message, passed to a `"%s"` format, and any other is
  one function per argument list its callers use. A `va_list` function is reached only
  through its variadic sibling.

A `static inline` function a header defines is bound as an exported one is: it is
allowlisted, and called through the raw binding generated for it, as
[`bindgen`](../../bindgen/SKILL.md)'s Generation section describes. The exception is a short
one whose whole implementation is in the header, which may be ported instead, to save the
cost of an FFI call, unless what it does depends on the build's features or configuration.
A reimplementation is a port, as [`porting`](../../porting/SKILL.md) describes, and is
annotated `Replaces`, as the [conventions](../../conventions/SKILL.md)' Anchors section describes.

Moved (exclusively or refcounted), borrowed (immutably or mutably), nullable, scalar and
array variants are separate functions when one signature cannot express every valid
contract. A function taking or returning type-erased arguments is generic.

A method is emitted in an `impl T` block on the type it implements, taking `&self` or
`&mut self` as its first argument. A free function stays free.

## 2. Globals

A global is bound as a `'static` borrow, never as an owner, its value taking the safe form
its type takes in a signature, as [Functions](#1-functions) describes. Its access
discipline follows from every C access:

- immutable after initialization: a shared handle;
- synchronized by C: the matching safe synchronization (an atomic, or guards handing out
  the shared or exclusive handle under the lock), never discarding a lock's status;
- otherwise mutable: `unsafe` accessors that exclude concurrent access, reported as such;
- thread-local: a handle borrowed for a closure on the current thread, neither `Send` nor
  `Sync`.

A lock counts only if every access takes it and it rejects same-thread re-entry. A global
C sets up in a routine, rather than in its definition, is reached through the safe API only
once that routine has run, however the binding ensures it.

## 3. Function pointers

content.content:
### `libgit2/deps/llhttp/api.c` wave 194 batch 0: `llhttp.c`'s types ahead of api.c

A wrap batch ahead of its consumer: `deps/llhttp/llhttp.c`'s five types, which api.c's
`port` waves use, bound in llhttp.c's own file, `src/libgit2/deps/llhttp/llhttp.rs`, which
its wave 238 ports. `st::llhttp__internal_s` is `Parser`, a `define_ctype!` layout with
`ParserRef` and `ParserMut`, and its typedefs `llhttp__internal_t`, `llhttp_t` and
`git_http_parser` are the aliases `InternalT`, `LlhttpT` and `HttpParser`. A parser owns
nothing and C keeps no pointer to one, so it is a plain value: `CZeroable`, with no owner or
policy; its constructor, `llhttp__internal_init` through `llhttp_init`, is the next batch's.
The closed enums `llhttp_errno`, `llhttp_method`, `llhttp_status` and `llhttp_type` are
`Errno`, `Method`, `Status` and `ParserType`, 185 variants over bindgen's constants with
fallible conversions and an `Unnamed*` error each, their typedefs aliases (`ErrnoT`, …).

The `fields` cell counts the 21 assigned. 15 have accessors: the fields api.c, http.c,
`transports/httpclient.c` and `transports/httpparser.c` touch. The other six, `_index`,
`_span_pos0`, `_span_cb0`, `_current`, `header_state` and `initial_message_completed`, only
llhttp.c's generated code reads or writes (`query structs --field-touchers`), and three of
them would send it through a wild pointer or out of a table if written from outside, so they
have none (`crustify/evolution/wrap-ahead-field-users`). The fields holding an enum's value
are read typed and fallibly, and raw (`*_raw`) as api.c's getters return them; the flag words
and `finish` raw, until `llhttp_flags`, `llhttp_lenient_flags` and `llhttp_finish` are bound.
`reason` is lent as a `&CStr` for the handle's borrow and set only from a `&'static CStr`;
`error_pos` is never followed, only compared with a caller's slice (`error_offset`); `data`
and `settings` are read as addresses and set through the batch's two `unsafe fn`s, whose
contracts carry what the callbacks read through them. Those four are the boundary scan's
sites in the changeset: no safe form replaces a user's untyped context, and `settings`'
typed getter waits for `llhttp_settings_s`, api.c's item, which the cycle through
`llhttp_cb` puts after this batch (T3 drops the cast edge). The pointer findings of the
struct's eight pointer fields, and `llhttp__internal_init`'s and `llhttp_init`'s `init`
roles, are in the ownership store.

The raw bindings gain `llhttp.h` in `wrapper.h`, the five types with their typedefs, and
api.c's `llhttp_init`, `llhttp_settings_init`, `llhttp_execute` and nine getters, which the
equivalence tests compare with; `llhttp_settings_s` and the callback typedefs come in with
them. Tests: 12 `unit_pub` (the enums' values and errors, every setter against its getter),
4 `ub_safe` (reborrows, a lent reason, parsers moved in a `Vec`), 6 `ub_unsafe` (one suite
per `unsafe` setter: callbacks reading the stored context through C, a context replaced
between calls, NULL settings, a table that ignores `data`), 8 `equiv` (two parsers fed the
same input by `llhttp_execute`, one read through api.c's getters and one through the
handles, compared after every step: a response in pieces, an unnamed status, requests with
their method and upgrade, an invalid message, a callback's own error, a pause and resume, the
lenient flags, the setters' effect on the C) and 5 compile-fail doctests. llhttp has no C
tests of its own in the tree.

Coverage was measured with `crustify/scripts/coverage/run.sh` on a `git archive` of the wave
tip `2216b0cd0` and on this tree, each suite alone, and read with `report.py` from the
scratch tree's `src/libgit2`, the unit column merging `lib` and `unit_pub`. The tip's Rust
figures are the recorded ones; its C figures read `27.92`% (`ub_safe`), `19.08`%
(`ub_unsafe`), `42.51`% (`equiv`), `31.37`% (unit) and `44.98`% (total), against which the pp
cells are taken. The C total moves
by `+1.12` pp: the equivalence and unsafe-setter tests run llhttp's parser, which nothing
reached before (`llhttp.c` 18.64% of lines, `http.c` 78.35%, `api.c` 11.99%). Worklist:
`llhttp.rs` 110 of 110 lines, 33 of 33 functions, 147 of 148 regions; the region missed,
`error_offset`'s return for a position before the slice, has an assertion added after the
measurement. Of the parser's states the tests reach the initialised, parsing, paused,
upgrade-paused and failed ones, and the transitions between them that the setters and
`llhttp_execute` make. The Overview's Rust LoC moves by ffimap's `code.loc.total` (`+919`)
and `code.tests.loc.total` (`+683`); `wrapped types` counts the five against the recorded
`258`.

The safety audit scans (ffimap `9aa2ef1`, `--ffibox`, `--sys-crates pcre2_sys`, the 13 seams,
`--regions ffi_import,ffi_export`): `pub raw ptr`, `pub void ptr` and `pub unsafe fn` are the
two getters and two setters above, `raw→std` the reason's `CStr::from_ptr`, `C by value`
three mentions of `llhttp__internal_s` by value in the layout and its handles' seams, and the
raw derefs and unsafe blocks the accessors' one-operation projections and reads. The four
`unsafe` blocks the first scan found outside the regions were the `Unnamed*` errors' `write!`
(std's `format_args!`, which ffimap counts); their `Display` writes its parts instead, as
`basics.rs`'s `UnnamedHashId` does. `ffimap api` against the tip: the five items are `new`, as
are all 212 anchor keys of the file (the 185 constants, 15 fields and 7 typedefs with them),
and every unattributed module is `kept` but the raw `sys::libgit2`, `extended`.

Gates, on the base `2216b0cd0`, the wave branch's tip when the batch landed: the workspace is
formatted, and `clippy --all-targets` passes with warnings denied on `plain`. The whole
workspace passes on `plain` (`lib` 840 and 1 ignored, `ub_safe` 766, `ub_unsafe` 126,
`equiv` 536, `unit_pub` 79, `hidden_symbols` 1, doctests 72 merged and 383 standalone). The
batch's tests pass under ASan+UBSan, and its `unit_pub` and `ub_safe` tests under Miri; each
`equiv` and `ub_unsafe` test was run alone there and stops at `llhttp_init` or
`llhttp_settings_init` (`calls C`). TSan has no obligation: no `Send` or `Sync` is asserted
and no thread added; nor has BSan, which nothing here is expected to trigger. The package
builds alone in bundled mode, with `glibc-bindings` and `ffibox` patched to their local
sources and CMake and pkg-config given the side campaigns' `plain` installs of OpenSSL, PCRE2

# A callback whose context is reached through an argument has no sound C form

Status: `open` (weighed by `wave-194/batch-2/run-1`; the spec change is not made).

## Signal

Skills that leave a case unspecified that a binding cannot settle well (`evolution` §2).
`binding-symbols`' Function pointers section builds a callable type's C half from "a C
function, with its context, which Rust calls … through an `unsafe` constructor whose
contract states … its context's lifetime and threads, and safe to call". For a function
pointer "without a context parameter" it says the Rust half carries no captured state. It
does not cover the case where C has no context parameter because the context lives in an
argument: there the C function's soundness depends on the argument, not on anything the
callable type holds, so a safe `call` with an arbitrary argument cannot be sound.

## Evidence

`wave-194/batch-1/run-1`: `llhttp_cb` (`int (*)(llhttp_t *)`) and `llhttp_data_cb` take no
context; their context is the parser's `data`, which libgit2's C callbacks
(`transports/httpclient.c`'s `on_header_field`, `on_body`, …) read as an
`http_parser_context *`. The batch's `Callback::from_fn` (`pub(crate)`) can only require
that the function be sound "with every live, exclusively held parser, whatever its `data`
and `settings` hold", which no such C callback meets: `Callback::call(Parser::new()…)`
would hand it a NULL `data`. The sound C form is the call made through the settings its
parser executes with, whose contract (`set_settings_ptr`) vouches for that parser; the
batch leaves that to the settings binding (api.c's `wrap`).

## Destination

The spec: `binding-symbols`, Function pointers, its three cases that shape the type.

## Change

Not made yet. `wave-194/batch-2/run-1`, the next batch that binds the table holding such
callbacks, weighed the two candidates and took the first, which needs no new primitive:

- the callable type's C half keeps the strong contract, sound with any argument whatever
  context it carries, and a C function that reads its context from an argument is never
  one, so `call` stays safe;
- a table of callables, bound as a layout whose slots are set only from the callable types,
  is sound with any object, and the object's setter that stores it is safe, taking a
  `'static` borrow where C keeps its address (`ParserMut::set_settings(Option<&'static
  Settings>)`);
- a table C builds of functions that read their context from the object is stored only
  through the object's `unsafe` setter, whose contract vouches for the object's context
  (`set_settings_ptr`), and is read back from the object as the address it holds, not as the
  table's handle, whose getters would hand out callables callable with any object; its
  functions are reached only through the routine of the object that dispatches them (api.c's
  `CALLBACK_MAYBE`, `port` in wave 195), with that object.

In `binding-symbols` § Function pointers, as a fourth case after "one without a context
parameter carries no captured state":

> - one whose context C reaches through another argument, such as the object it is
>   handed, has a C half only for functions sound with any such argument. A C function
>   that reads its context there is reached only through the object that holds it, by the
>   routine that dispatches it with that object, never as the callable type: a field or
>   table that holds such functions is set from C, or through an `unsafe` setter whose
>   contract carries the object's context, and read back as no callable.

## Evidence (`wave-194/batch-2/run-1`)

`llhttp_settings_s`, bound as `Settings` in `src/libgit2/deps/llhttp/api.rs`: its 23 slots
are set from `Callback` / `DataCallback` only, read back as them through the handles'
invariant (each non-NULL slot is one `from_fn` accepts), and `Settings` is `Send` and
`Sync`, so that a `static` holds one, as libgit2's `httpclient.c` does in C. `ParserRef`'s
`settings` getter stays the raw address: `transports/httpclient.c`'s `on_header_field`,
`on_body` and the others cast `parser->data` to `http_parser_context *`, so a
`SettingsRef` over that table would let `Settings`' getter return a `DataCallback` whose
safe `call(Parser::new().as_mut(), …)` hands them a NULL context.

## Validation

None run.

## Review

None yet.
# A callback can re-enter the function that calls it, through the object it is handed

Status: `open`.

## Signal

A rule the how-to skills lack, which a binding had to work out by hand (`evolution` §2).
`binding-symbols`' Function pointers section has a trampoline refuse "a re-entrant call,
which would alias an `FnMut` closure": the hazard it names is the closure's state. It says
nothing of the function that runs the callback, whose own state the callback can reach when
C hands it the object the function is working on. Re-entering that function, or resetting
the object, from the callback is then undefined behaviour in C, reachable from safe Rust.

## Evidence

`wave-194/batch-1/run-1` (`deps/llhttp/llhttp.c`'s `llhttp__internal_execute`, bound as
`ParserMut::parse`). The parser's settings name callbacks C calls with the parser being
parsed, so a Rust handler receives that parser's exclusive handle, from which a safe API
offers `parse` and `reinit`. A nested `llhttp__internal_execute` on the same parser sets
`_span_pos0` into the nested input and moves `_index`; the outer run, resuming after the
callback, then hands a span callback `(state->_span_pos0, p)` across two allocations (a
wild length), and `llparse__match_sequence*` index their blobs with the nested `_index`.
`llhttp__internal_init` from a callback nulls `_span_pos0`, which a span-end state reads
back as its start. The batch refuses both with a panic, through a thread-local register of
the parsers each thread is executing, which the trampolines' barrier turns into the
callback's error (`tests/ub_unsafe/deps/llhttp/llhttp.rs`,
`a_handler_cannot_parse_the_parser_whose_parse_runs_it`,
`a_handler_cannot_initialise_the_parser_whose_parse_runs_it`).

## Destination

The spec: `binding-symbols`, Function pointers, beside the trampoline's re-entry rule; and
`analysis`' Findings, which should list it as something the analysis establishes.

## Change

Not made yet. In `binding-symbols` § Function pointers, after the paragraph on the
trampoline's re-entry refusal:

> A function that calls a callback with an object it is working on lends that object to
> the callback. The analysis establishes which of the object's routines C allows from
> within the callback; a routine it does not, the function itself or one that resets the
> state the function resumes from, is refused there by the binding, on the thread that
> runs the function, since the callback holds an exclusive handle the borrow checker
> cannot tell from any other.

In `analysis` § Findings, under states and transitions: "the calls a callback may make on
the object its caller lends it, and those that would corrupt the caller's state".

## Validation

None run: the rule is the one this batch followed; a rerun of the batch under it would
produce the same binding. The batch's two UB tests above, run under ASan+UBSan, Miri (they
stop at the foreign call) and BSan alone, are its evidence that the refusal holds.

## Review

None yet.

Author: Marius Momeu <marius.momeu@berkeley.edu>
Date:   Fri Nov 13 18:45:30 2026 +0000

    utf8.c: port 5 items (wave-229/batch-0/run-1)
    
    glb::utf8proc_utf8class
    fn::utf8_charlen
    fn::git_utf8_iterate
    fn::git_utf8_char_length
    fn::git_utf8_valid_buf_length
    
    The module's whole port, waves 229 to 231 folded into one batch. The
    table is a static built by a const fn from its lead-byte ranges;
    utf8_charlen is the private sequence_len; the three functions are the
    native decode_char(&[u8]) -> Result<(char, usize), InvalidCodePoint>,

### `libgit2/src/util/utf8.c` integration: the switch from C

The campaign's first switch, run by `modules/libgit2/src/util/utf8.c/integration/run-1` on the
module's branch after the merge of the working branch (`43605086f`): `012d1d34c`, and the
fork's `1b37e3d08`. The export feature `ffi-export-src-util-utf8-c` is deleted, the crate's
only one, so `utf8.rs`'s gateway compiles from now on, and its four `unit_priv` tests run in
`lib`. The module's six `equiv` tests are retired with the C they compared
(`tests/equiv/src/util/utf8.rs`); their cases stay in its unit tests and doctests. The raw
bindings of `git_utf8_iterate`, `git_utf8_char_length` and `git_utf8_valid_buf_length` stay,
and now reach the exports. `src/util/utf8.c` leaves `c/`: the change is the commit
`integrate src/util/utf8.c` on a local `fork/main`, which stands for
`crustify-rs/libgit2-fork`'s `main` and is not pushed, and `.gitmodules` names the fork.
`utf8.h` stays for `path.c`, `diff_xdiff.c` and `fs_path.c`. The module's tied C test,
`tests/util/utf8.c`, calls `git_utf8_char_length` alone, so it stays and checks the export.
No C test leaves, so no case needs listing. The exports are a private module's, so the
crate's API does not change.

The switch also made the one-time change of the C build. The fork's
`cmake/SelectRust.cmake` links the static library that `LIBGIT2_RUST_LIBRARY` names wherever
the remaining C is linked: `libgit2.so`, the CLI, `libgit2_tests` and `util_tests`. It is an
imported target among `LIBGIT2_SYSTEM_LIBS`. `libgit2.so` keeps the Rust's symbols local
(`--exclude-libs`). Its dynamic symbols are the previous generation's on every variant,
`asan-ubsan`'s two linker-made `__start_`/`__stop_asan_globals` aside. Those come from LLVM
23's instrumentation of the Rust and are protected. Without the variable, the library leaves
the three exports undefined, as the crate's bundled and shared builds of `c/` need. Each
variant's `build` command first makes the library (`crustify/scripts/rust-staticlib.sh`),
between `configure` and the C's link. It builds the crate of the checkout that runs it as a
`staticlib` on the dev profile, the profile the Rust tests run on, so that the C tests check
the same build with debug assertions and overflow checks on. It builds in campaign mode
against the configured variant, with `--features bindgen`, so that the committed bindings
are checked, and with `CRUSTIFY_STATICLIB`, under which `build.rs` reads the build's
configuration and links none of its C. It instruments the Rust as `cargo-variant.sh` does.
`nm` shows that the library defines only the Rust, the three exports and the crate's
`__extern` wrappers, and no libgit2 C. Every other campaign build leaves the library out of
its link, matched by canonical path, so that no binary holds the Rust twice. BSan has no
`cargo bsan rustc`, so a stand-in for the cargo it runs turns its `build` into `rustc
--crate-type staticlib`. The BSan runtime its driver bundles is removed from the copy, since
the variant's C link links it.

The variants were rebuilt as a new generation, `crustify/builds.gen1`, with
`crustify/scripts/build-variants.sh`, and this worktree's `crustify/builds` links to it.
`crustify/builds` itself, which three batches were using, was left untouched. Each variant is
configured from the generation's own `c`, a detached worktree of the fork at `1b37e3d08`, so
that the build outlives this worktree and the base checkout's next moves (`build.json`
version 7). Each archive holds 212 objects, where the previous generation's held 213:
`utf8.c.o` is gone. Each variant passed its smoke test (`util_tests -sutf8`). In every
variant, `utf8proc_utf8class` is absent from the C test executables, which take
`git_utf8_iterate` from the Rust; in `libgit2.so` it is a local symbol.

Gates on `012d1d34c`, over gen1, from `end-gates` snapshots at 24 jobs. The workspace is
formatted, and `clippy --workspace --all-targets` passes with warnings denied. Plain passes
the whole workspace: `lib` 848 and 1 ignored, `equiv` 528, `ub_safe` 763, `ub_unsafe` 120,
`unit_pub` 84, `hidden_symbols` 1, doctests 76 and 378. ASan+UBSan and TSan pass it but for
the known nightly failures: the 9 `compile_fail` snapshots and the `CommitBuilder` doctest
(E0624). Miri passes every binary: `lib` 400, `ub_safe` 194, `equiv` 38, `unit_pub` 49,
`ub_unsafe` 19, the rest marked. The remaining C tests ran over the link with the Rust,
through `crustify/scripts/c-tests.sh`. It runs `build.json`'s `ctest` command, then every
suite alone as the baseline did, and compares the result with `c-baseline.json`. Plain,
ASan+UBSan and TSan give 3443 passed and 55 skipped of 3498, coverage 3444 and 54, each the
baseline's record. Under TSan, the same 10 suites as the baseline's report the C's
lock-order inversions and races, and no case fails; no report has a Rust frame. `ctest`
passes both targets on plain, ASan+UBSan and coverage. Under TSan it fails `offline` on those
reports alone, 49 lock-order inversions and glibc's `tzset` race. BSan was rebuilt and not
run, as the settings' `sanitizers` answer has it. `c/` changed, so the crate was packaged as
`package-gate-procedure` has it. The package has 697 files, `utf8.c` out and
`SelectRust.cmake` in, and builds alone in bundled mode. Its `libgit2.pc`'s
`Requires.private` also needs the side campaigns' installs on `PKG_CONFIG_PATH`, beside
`CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH`. Its `lib` tests link, `path.c`'s `next_hfs_char` calling the Rust export.
790 pass, among them the module's; the other 58 need the fixture repositories of
`c/tests/resources`, which the package leaves out.

From the switch on, the module's coverage is its Rust's: `utf8.c` is in no build, and the C
figures lose its 71 lines. This run did not measure coverage. The procedure this switch
worked out, which every later switch repeats, is proposed for the spec
(`crustify/evolution/module-switch-procedure`). That libgit2's switch removes a file and no
CMake line is a lesson. Usage cells are the assistant's.

`deps/ntlmclient/compat.h` is a header with no translation unit, and its one scheduled item is
`#define MIN(x, y) (((x) < (y)) ? (x) : (y))`, under `#ifndef MIN`; the header's `bool`,
`true` and `false` are defined only under `_MSC_VER`. `mac::MIN` is the native

# wavefront

Wavefront answers deterministic queries about a C codebase, its entities, their uses and
dependencies, their pointers and lifecycles, and generates dependency-ordered wave plans
over it.

It is the first resort for any question about the C codebase: an entity's definition,
fields or signature, its users, callers and casts, what it depends on, and the pointer
findings and lifecycle roles submitted on it are queried rather than searched for in the
source, so that each answer covers every site the traced build compiles, and every query
of one fact gets one answer. The source is read where wavefront records nothing, to read a
body, and to judge what wavefront records.

Its `README.md` and `--help` are read in full before its first command, and each section
below names the documents under its `docs/` that its stage reads, also in full. How
wavefront scopes, orders and batches, what its configuration, tables and records hold, and
what each query returns are those documents', and are not restated here. Its goals and
non-goals, `docs/goals.md`, are what a change to wavefront is judged against, as
[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes.

## Campaign state

Wavefront's repo root is the C root: it is passed `<workdir>/c`, so that every path it
reads and reports is relative to the C root, as the plan records them. Its state sits
under `crustify/wavefront/`, which the configuration names as its `state_dir`,
`../crustify/wavefront`:

- `codeql/`, the CodeQL database and its T1/T2 tables, and `.cache`, both gitignored;
- `configs/wavefront-config.json`, the campaign's configuration, which every query of the
  bindings and reviews resolves through, with `"t3_dir": "t3"`;
- `t3/`, the T3 tables, one campaign-wide pair; and
- `ownership-store.json`, the findings submitted to it through the CLI. A finding
  submitted once is queried again rather than re-derived.

The configuration's `modules` hold one record per module of `modules.json`, named
`<link-unit>/<name>`, with ` (foundational)` after a foundational module's name.

What follows is how wavefront serves each stage: each section names the skill and section
it adds to, and states only what wavefront adds there.

## Setup

### Setup › Provisioning

CodeQL and wavefront's query pack dependencies are installed, as its README describes.
`crustify/.gitignore` lists `wavefront/codeql` and `wavefront/.cache`.

### Setup › Artifact tree

`crustify/wavefront/` is scaffolded for wavefront's state.

### Setup › Baseline

Once the builds and the baseline are recorded, the CodeQL database is created from a
traced build of the `plain` configuration in a fresh scratch dir, with `c/` as its source
root, and its T1/T2 tables are extracted, through a bootstrap configuration in
`crustify/tmp/`; the campaign's own configuration is the plan's.

## Planning

Planning reads `docs/scoping.md`, `docs/graph.md`, `docs/batching.md`,
`docs/type-lifecycle.md`, `docs/artifacts/t3.md` and `docs/artifacts/schedule.md`.

### Decomposition › Runs

Each planner run brings the configuration and the T3 tables up to date with the plan: it
emits what is missing, migrates what follows an earlier wavefront schema, adds what the
scope adds and corrects what is wrong. A changed configuration or T3 row changes the graph,
so the `todo` waves whose batches it moves are re-planned, and the `depends_on` in
`modules.json` when it moves them.

### Decomposition › Dependencies

The configuration's `modules` are authored from `modules.json`: each module's files, with
the entities its `items` list select, each by the kind it is in C. Wavefront refuses an
entry that claims what its file only declares, and a unit two modules claim, so that every
entity is owned by exactly one module; the configuration is verified against the CLI.

A module's dependency records are counted from a schedule of the whole closure, without

`unique_edges` and `total_edges`; its items give the `counters`, and their references

### Decomposition › Foundational modules

The foundational modules' candidates are selected from the configuration's graph, after
the T3 tables are written, so that their cast edges resolve type-erased values: the

the foundational modules find it.

### Scheduling › Order

The link units and modules are ordered from the configuration, after its T3 tables are

- every type-erased parameter and field with no cast, followed until it is read as a named

  compilation hides from the traced build.
